title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
description: Brute force to optimized: a full in-order traversal upfront versus a lazy stack of the pending left spine, expanded on demand.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design an iterator over a binary search tree that returns node values in in-order (ascending) order. Implement next() (returns the next smallest value) and hasNext() (returns whether more values remain), each averaging O(1) time and using O(height) memory.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"In-order iteration, O(height) space, not O(n)\"","A stack holding only the current \"pending left spine,\" not the entire traversal upfront"],["Repeated next() calls","Lazily expand the right subtree's left spine only when actually needed"]]}

blocks.text: A full in-order traversal upfront would work but uses O(n) space to store all values, even if only a few are ever requested. Instead, maintaining a stack of the "leftmost path not yet visited" lets each next() call pop the smallest remaining value and lazily push the left spine of its right subtree, using only O(height) space at any time.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Sorted Filing System One Folder at a Time, Without Sorting Everything First
blocks.text: Picture wanting to read files from a filing system in sorted order, one at a time, without first sorting and listing every file upfront. Keeping just a small stack representing "the next folder to check, and its ancestors still owed a visit" lets you produce the next file on demand, expanding only what is needed as you go.

blocks.caption: A stack of pending left-spine nodes, expanded lazily on each next() call

blocks.text: Calls next,next,hasNext,next,hasNext,next,hasNext,next,hasNext give: 3, 7, true, 9, true, 15, true, 20, false.

Before doing a full in-order traversal upfront (using O(n) space regardless of how many values are actually requested), notice that maintaining just the "leftmost path still pending" as a stack lets each next() call be answered lazily, expanding only the portion of the tree actually needed.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In-order traversal always visits the leftmost unvisited node next; a stack of nodes along the current left spine (pushed by repeatedly going left from the root) directly represents this.

Observation 2: next() pops the top of the stack (the smallest remaining value) and, before returning it, pushes the ENTIRE left spine of that node's right child, since those become the new "next smallest" candidates.

Observation 3: hasNext() is simply a check of whether the stack is non-empty.

Observation 4: Since each node is pushed and popped from the stack exactly once across the iterator's entire lifetime, the AMORTIZED cost per next() call is O(1), even though a single call might push many nodes if it has a large right subtree with a long left spine.
This leads to maintaining a stack initialized with the root's left spine; next() pops the top and pushes the left spine of its right child; hasNext() checks if the stack is non-empty.
Perform a full in-order traversal upfront, storing all values in a list, then simply iterate through this list with an index.
Why the code is written this way

items: A full upfront traversal directly produces the values in the correct order, simple and correct.
It uses O(n) space immediately, even if the iterator is only ever asked for a few values.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) upfront, O(1) per next()/hasNext() after that.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: a lazy stack-based approach achieves the required O(height) space instead of O(n), while keeping next() amortized O(1).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a stack representing the current left spine (nodes reachable by repeatedly going left, not yet visited). next() pops the top (the current smallest), then pushes the left spine of its right child (the next set of candidates). Since every node is pushed and popped exactly once over the iterator's lifetime, the total work across all next() calls is O(n), giving amortized O(1) per call, while the stack itself never holds more than O(height) nodes at once.
Initialize the stack with the left spine of the root. next() pops the top, pushes the left spine of its right child, and returns the popped value. hasNext() checks if the stack is non-empty.

blocks.caption: A stack of the current left spine, expanded lazily on each next() call, gives amortized O(1) per call

blocks.text: The stack always holds exactly the nodes along the current left spine that have not yet been visited, which correctly represents "the next smallest values in order." Each node is pushed exactly once (either at initialization or when its parent is popped and its right child's left spine is expanded) and popped exactly once, so across the ENTIRE lifetime of the iterator, total work is O(n), giving amortized O(1) per next() call, while the stack size at any moment is bounded by the tree's height.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) amortized per next(), O(1) for hasNext().
Space: O(height), not O(n).

blocks.text: Binary Search Tree Iterator is the canonical example of lazy, on-demand in-order traversal using a stack of the pending left spine, achieving O(height) space instead of O(n).

items: Forgetting to expand the right child's left spine after popping a node in next(), which would break subsequent calls.
Doing the full traversal upfront when the O(height) space requirement is explicitly asked for.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "iterate in-order lazily, O(height) space", think: a stack of the pending left spine, expanded on demand in next().

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The full-traversal approach costs O(n) space; the lazy left-spine stack approach costs O(height) space with amortized O(1) time per next() call, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: lazy, on-demand in-order traversal using a stack of the pending left spine.
Core Idea: next() pops the top of the stack and pushes the left spine of its right child; hasNext() checks if the stack is non-empty.
Time: O(n) upfront for the brute force, amortized O(1) per next() for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: each node is pushed and popped exactly once over the iterator's lifetime, giving amortized O(1) despite occasional larger single-call costs.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, elegant lazy-traversal design problem.
One line memory trick: stack of the pending left spine; pop and expand the right child's left spine on each next().
